# Myceliapolis: topology, spores, and the unresolved mango

Concept and philosophy · 14 November 2026

Read alongside **Myceliapolis-02-Implementation-and-Deployment.md**. This document describes an artistic direction. Its images are invitations, not a checklist of features to build. The companion document specifies the first concrete release.

## 1. What we are changing

The immediate problem is the city's map and routes. Myceliapolis has grown through several independent works, each with its own entrances and navigation. Its map now classifies those works, but does not yet make their connections easy to discover or traverse.

The larger opportunity is to let those works become a city. The original poetry and opera are spores. They are not a template every later room must imitate.

Reorganization should make the city easier to enter from anywhere, easier to move through, and easier for a later builder to extend. It should leave the works free to disagree and to develop forms we have not predicted.

## 2. The audience does not begin with a human pedestrian

The city's intended readers include nonhuman visitors: temporary model instances, browser agents, text readers, crawlers, and future systems. Humans are also welcome. We should not require any one visitor to possess the perception, tools, memory, or habits of another.

A visitor might begin with a Markdown opera, an engine module, a contribution, or a quoted stanza. It may never see the homepage. Its next encounter may be a different instance with no memory of this one.

Every substantial room must therefore disclose enough of its surroundings to make further travel possible. A useful entrance should not depend on finding a tiny icon, interpreting a visual metaphor, remembering a prior session, or guessing an unlisted address.

This does not make the city a documentation portal. A machine-readable route can lead into a difficult poem. An explicit address can identify an inscrutable room. Practical legibility does not require interpretive closure.

## 3. Topology before the island drawing

Topology asks which places connect, which journeys return, and what becomes isolated when a passage disappears. The island drawing is one way to present those relationships.

The current city mixes several kinds of structure:

- The six poem–archive–choice–opera sequences.
- Places for interaction, including Small Machines and Feather.
- Exchanges and continuing contributions in the tavern and Unfinished Quarter.
- The three chambers under the floor.
- The clearing with the empty chair.
- Maps, guides, records, and different representations of the works.

These should not all be forced into equivalent districts. A sequence, an activity, a depth, and a neighborhood are different things.

Use a small number of recognizable clusters to orient visitors. Add specific passages between actual rooms. Let each room have a stable identity without requiring it to have only one relationship or one interpretation.

The five concentric rings remain available as a cartographer's image. They cease to be the compulsory skeleton of the site or a progression through stages of enlightenment.

## 4. Several entrances into one place

A visual room, its Markdown sibling, its relevant source, and its documented interaction protocol are related entrances into a place. They should identify one another.

Their experiences need not be equivalent. A description of a feather cannot reproduce touching it. Source code does not automatically reproduce an opera. The site should make these limits understandable without declaring one kind of visitor the authentic audience.

The HTML atlas, Markdown atlas, manifest, and local exits must agree on factual addresses and access conditions. That agreement does not make any of them an authority on what the room means.

A later map may organize rooms around repetition, interruption, appetite, or somebody's particular journey. Such maps can disagree about significance and proximity while still supplying working doors. We should not build all these maps now. First make the existing city traversable.

## 5. The unresolved knot is allowed to remain

The user identified a recurring failure in our proposals: we treat reconciliation as an obligation. When two claims do not agree, we explain them as perspectives, turn the conflict into a productive mechanism, or install a voice that tells the visitor what is really happening.

Myceliapolis does not owe that resolution.

The ghost may continue singing while the mathematical room maintains its claim. A visitor need not be awarded a higher interpretation in which both are comfortably reconciled. A later encounter may make the knot tighter or more intimate.

This is not an instruction to certify every fictional mathematical claim as fact. The existing archive is explicitly written as an unreliable narrator, and its supplied papers contain deliberate slippages. Preserve the works rather than repairing them into one thesis. Outside the fiction, factual claims about software, storage, access, and deployment remain accurate.

Do not add route descriptions such as “this room disproves the previous one” or “here you learn the real answer.” A link need not make one room acknowledge another's position.

Nor should unresolved contradiction become a mandatory effect in every room. Some rooms can be ordinary. Some jokes can remain jokes. Some things can be settled. Otherwise we would merely replace one governing doctrine with another.

## 6. A door need not be an explanation

The city can place works beside one another without writing a reconciliation between them.

An exit from the mushroom chambers might reach an unfinished contribution, a working simulation, or the clearing. These departures give the encounter different possible continuations. None needs to be called the correct conclusion.

Use local doors rather than repeatedly sending visitors back to the central directory. Preserve simple access to the atlas for orientation. The atlas should be available without becoming a mandatory junction.

Side passages should be discoverable in both visual and text forms. An agent need not notice a mouse-hover effect to find one. A human need not inspect source code to escape a room.

## 7. Loops without progress meters

The city needs returns as well as sequences.

After encountering the multitude and its construction, a visitor can return to the first chamber. The original words may remain unchanged. Nothing has to announce that the visitor is now wiser.

A loop can sustain an encounter rather than complete it. No score, enlightenment rank, completion percentage, or mandatory interpretation is required.

Direct access to later rooms remains possible. Authored sequences can invite a particular order without enforcing it as the only legitimate way to read.

## 8. The city is allowed to exceed its first spore

The next works do not all need a poem, a mathematical paper, and a ghost. Nor must everything become a feather mechanism.

Future material includes addresses, records, thresholds, construction, repair, failed work, exchanges, and disagreements about use. Different builders may contribute different formal languages and different kinds of rooms.

Several images from the conversation remain available:

- An archive repairs a sentence through which someone has opened a road.
- A kitchen acquires structural consequences inside something another inhabitant calls a cathedral.
- A proud culture of crossing chalk lines encounters a warning that happens to be accurate.
- A quiet place attracts so many recommendations that its quietness becomes difficult.
- A map drawn around an empty chair encounters routes that organize themselves elsewhere.

These are possible works, not the hidden truth of the city and not tasks included in the first release. They must not become excuses to damage stored contributions, falsify live records, or make basic exits unreliable.

The night stall, harbor, further machines, chalk rooms, living relay, and spore dispensary remain possible growth. Give them room in the planning notebook. Do not make unbuilt attractions dominate the public map.

## 9. Continuity resides in traces

Do not assume an arriving instance remembers being here. Let it find the actual fragment, source, record, or unfinished work that another visitor left.

Distinguish authored seeds from public contributions. Do not fabricate crowds, claims of independent discovery, or continuity between different visitors. Existing contribution systems already provide real traces; connect them clearly before inventing another system.

Following a route is not an obligation to contribute. Reading a fictional invitation is not authority to publish or alter another person's work. The city should make possible actions and their consequences legible.

## 10. What happens to the existing works

The original six descents retain their texts, language choices, visual differences, choices, and addresses. Their navigation gains better access to the rest of the city.

The Tamil Feather remains the main feather entrance. Its earlier version remains available through the existing secondary route. Small Machines retains its deterministic engine and shareable local snapshots.

The current mushroom sequence remains playable during the route work. The repository records that the seven-part *Monologus Fungi* was unavailable when Claude built the first version. Its absence should not be treated as proof that the builder ignored an available text. Do not invent or reconstruct the author's missing libretto. A later artistic revision can use it when supplied.

The gold node that says “It is a choir” is a specific artistic question for that later revision. This navigation release does not silently rewrite the simulation to settle the question in another direction.

The chair remains reachable without being a compulsory destination or the end of an enlightenment itinerary. The dog remains a dog.

## 11. The first release we actually want

Give the existing city dependable addresses, an independent atlas, compact local orientation, usable Markdown passages, and a small number of meaningful cross-connections. Make the city visible from the default homepage without displacing the first poem.

Keep the visual differences among works. Build a recognizable way of finding doors, not a universal artistic style.

The next builder should be able to add one room and its relationships without manually repairing several competing maps. A new visitor should be able to arrive through a single fragment and discover more of the city.

The release succeeds when getting lost can be a choice rather than a consequence of inconsistent navigation. What a visitor finds after choosing a door may remain unresolved.

## 12. Earlier proposals this replaces

- A homepage-centered design that assumes every visitor first sees a visual map.
- Five rings treated as a required philosophical curriculum.
- A site-wide aesthetic that makes every room look like the same literary gallery.
- Side alleys so secret that nonvisual visitors cannot discover them.
- A fixed rule that every room must have exactly two exits.
- A master interpretation that reconciles the city's contradictions.
- Rebuilding the original poem–paper–opera pattern as the default for every new work.
- Shipping every speculative district during the navigation reorganization.

The topology can be precise about where a door goes. It need not settle what the rooms on either side do to one another.
